lead: A deployment model says who owns the hardware under your workload and who else shares it. It is a separate question from the service model: infrastructure, platform and software as a service say where you cut the stack, while public, private, hybrid and community say who holds the machines and who else stands on them. Every organisation picks one whenever it decides where a workload should live: a hospital's patient records, a group of colleges' examination portal, a shop's festive-season sale traffic.
prereq: You need: the five essential characteristics from chapter 1.3 and the service-model cuts from chapter 1.6.

sections.h3: Public and private: who owns the pool

blocks.text: A public cloud is owned by a provider that sells capacity to anyone who signs up. Many customers, called tenants, share the same physical servers, and virtualization keeps them apart. You rent by the hour or by the gigabyte and pay only for what you use. The sharing is the whole point: one provider's spare capacity becomes every customer's cheap capacity.

A private cloud is a pool owned or leased by one organisation and used by that organisation alone. It can sit on the company's own premises or be hosted by a vendor on dedicated hardware. Ownership brings control: you choose the hardware, the network paths, the patch schedule and the exact building where data is stored. It also brings the bill. The machines are capital cost, paid whether they are busy or idle, and someone on your payroll must run them.

A private cloud still has to be a cloud. It needs the essential characteristics from chapter 1.3: pooling, self-service, elasticity and metering. Without them, a room of servers is traditional hosting with a newer name.

sections.h3: Hybrid: a private core with public capacity on tap

blocks.text: A hybrid cloud joins two or more distinct clouds, usually a private core and a public provider, with a secure link such as a VPN or a dedicated interconnect. The link is not decoration. The workload itself must be able to move from one side to the other.

The usual pattern is cloud bursting. Base load runs on private hardware you already own. When demand crosses a threshold, extra instances start in the public cloud, take the overflow, and shut down when the spike ends. The private side keeps the sensitive data; the public side supplies only capacity.

Bursting needs preparation: the same virtual machine image or container on both sides, the data the burst needs reachable from both sides, and a threshold that triggers scale-out. The service models of chapter 1.6 do not change. Only the owner of the hardware changes.

A community cloud is shared by several organisations with a common concern: a group of colleges pooling an examination portal, or hospitals under one regulator pooling a records exchange. Members split the cost and the governance. It is cheaper than each member building a private cloud and more controlled than a public one, but the hard part is human: who operates it, who pays, and whose service level agreement wins.

A virtual private cloud (VPC) is a private slice carved out of public hardware: your own subnets, routing and firewalls inside a provider's network. It gives isolation, not ownership. The hardware is still shared and still the provider's, so a VPC is not a private cloud.

Multi-cloud means using two or more public providers, for lock-in cover or for a region the first provider does not serve. Federated and intercloud arrangements, where separate clouds trade resources across providers, appear in only a few syllabi; see Unit 4.

spec.title: Hybrid bursting: 3-day camp
spec.aria: A downward flow: the private core's 300 requests per second meets a 2,000 requests per second camp peak, a shortfall of 1,700 carried by 10 rented servers of 170 each for 72 hours at ₹30 per server-hour, giving ₹21,600, with a dashed branch to buying the servers for ₹8,00,000.

examples.question: A hospital chain runs a private data centre that serves 300 requests per second. Its appointment site normally handles 200 requests per second, but during a 3-day health camp it must handle 2,000 requests per second. Buying 10 extra servers to cover that peak costs ₹80,000 each. Renting 10 servers in a public cloud costs ₹30 per server-hour. Find (a) the capital cost of covering the peak in-house, (b) the cost of bursting for the 3 days, (c) the saving, and (d) the bursting cost over 3 years if the camp happens once a year.
steps: Peak shortfall = 2,000 − 300 = 1,700 requests per second. Ten servers carry this, so each server carries 1,700 ÷ 10 = 170 requests per second.
Capital cost of 10 servers = 10 × ₹80,000 = ₹8,00,000. These servers would sit idle for 362 days a year.
Burst duration = 3 days × 24 hours per day = 72 hours.
Burst cost = 10 servers × 72 hours × ₹30 per server-hour = ₹21,600.
Over 3 years the camp bursts 3 times: 3 × ₹21,600 = ₹64,800, still far below the one-time ₹8,00,000.
examples.answer: Bursting costs ₹21,600 against ₹8,00,000 of capital, a saving of ₹7,78,400; three years of bursting costs ₹64,800.

traps: Calling any server room a private cloud. It still needs pooling, self-service, elasticity and metering; without them it is traditional hosting.
Mixing the deployment model with the service model. 'We buy SaaS, so we are on a public cloud' does not follow, because a SaaS product can run in a private or community cloud.
Treating hybrid as any two clouds. The parts must be joined by a secure link and a real workload must move between them.
Believing a VPC is a private cloud. Isolation is not ownership; the hardware stays shared and provider-owned.
Forgetting that a community cloud has closed membership and shared governance. It is not a public cloud with a discount.

quiz.q: Name the four deployment models and the single question they all answer.
quiz.a: Public, private, hybrid and community. Each answers who owns the hardware and who else shares it.

quiz.q: In which model does a provider own the hardware and many unrelated tenants share it?
A firm has 40 servers in its own basement, each application pinned to fixed machines, and an engineer provisions every new server by hand. Why is this not a private cloud?
quiz.a: It lacks pooling, self-service, elasticity and metering. Resources are assigned permanently and a person does each allocation, so it is traditional hosting.

quiz.q: State in two sentences what cloud bursting is and what must be true before it works.
quiz.a: Base load runs on private hardware and the peak runs on public instances that start at a threshold and stop afterwards. Both sides need the same image, shared access to the data, and a secure link between them.

quiz.q: A private data centre serves 400 requests per second. A festival drives demand to 1,600 requests per second for 2 days. Each extra server carries 150 requests per second and rents at ₹25 per server-hour. How many servers must burst, and what does that cost?
quiz.a: Shortfall = 1,600 − 400 = 1,200 requests per second. Servers = 1,200 ÷ 150 = 8. Duration = 2 × 24 = 48 hours. Cost = 8 × 48 × ₹25 = ₹9,600.

quiz.q: Two teams both claim to be hybrid. Team A runs a private cloud and, separately, a public SaaS email account. Team B runs a private core with a VPN into a public provider, and its web tier scales out there every evening. Which is hybrid, and why?
quiz.a: Team B. Hybrid needs a secure join and a workload that actually moves between the two sides. Team A has two unrelated clouds, which is coexistence or multi-cloud, not hybrid.

quiz.q: Twelve colleges want one examination portal for 60,000 students, results published twice a year, and each college has very little capital. Which deployment model fits, and what is the main risk?
quiz.a: A community cloud: shared cost and shared control over student data, sized for a twice-yearly peak. The main risk is governance: who operates it, who pays, and whose service level agreement applies on results day.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the debate has moved from which model to where data may legally sit: payment-data localisation rules pushed banks and payment firms towards India-region hosting, and 'sovereign cloud' offerings now sell exactly that promise. Hybrid landing zones, a governed private network extended into a public provider, are standard in large enterprises. Research moves towards federated and intercloud arrangements (Unit 4) and confidential computing, where a public tenant's data stays encrypted even from the provider. Search 'cloud bursting', 'sovereign cloud', 'data localisation RBI' and 'landing zone'.
